name: ABBA: Against the Odds
description:
A Business Analysis of Cultural Permanence
Most pop groups from the 1970s are nostalgia acts or forgotten footnotes. ABBA became a billion-dollar empire that grows stronger with each generation.
This series applies the same investigative rigor and business analysis I bring to political accountability work—but examines creation instead of corruption, success instead of failure, joy instead of malice.
How did four Swedish musicians crack the code of multi-generational relevance? What strategic decisions separated them from thousands of equally talented contemporaries who faded into obscurity? Why does their music work for both 8-year-olds and 80-year-olds simultaneously?
We'll examine the musical formula, video innovation, business model, relationship dynamics, and the longevity factors that turned a Eurovision novelty act into a cultural phenomenon still generating over $100 million annually fifty years later.
Because excellence that endures isn't accidental—it's designed.

name: Afghanistan: The Eternal Battleground
description: A New York Times article about children starving after U.S. aid cuts prompted a question: How long has Afghanistan been suffering? The answer: 2,500 years. From the Achaemenid Persians to Alexander the Great, from Genghis Khan's apocalyptic destruction to the British Empire's three failed invasions, from Soviet occupation to American abandonment - Afghanistan has been invaded, occupied, and devastated almost continuously throughout recorded history. The brief periods of genuine peace add up to less than 10% of that time. This ten-part series traces every empire that made the same mistakes in Afghanistan, causing the same civilian suffering, and learning nothing from those who came before. Those starving children in 2026 aren't an aberration - they're the latest victims in history's longest tragedy, and the first to die not from war, but from aid cuts after dependency was created.

name: America's Next Industrial Revolution
description: An Ongoing Series on EVs, AI, and Robotics

name: An Oligarch Review
description:
When private power rivals the state, who checks it?

The Atlantic asked readers to choose between two overlords, Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. This series declines the choice and widens the field.

Over thirteen essays and a conclusion, it measures the private citizens whose fortunes now do what only governments used to do, from Russia's 1990s bankers and America's robber barons to Zuckerberg, Thiel, Murdoch, the Kochs, Gates, Soros, Canada's quiet dynasties and California's billionaire-tax fight.

Each is scored on the same five tests, the Overlord Index: Chokepoints, Megaphone, Purchase, Defiance and Impunity. Start with the Introduction, where the rubric and the full series index sit.

name: Canada: How the Dominion Was Forged
short: Canada: How the Dominion Was Forged
sections: Canada: How the Dominion Was Forged
aliases: Canada: How the Dominion Was Forged
description:
In April 2026, a modest banker named Mark Carney — a man who had never held elected office sixteen months earlier — clinched a majority government by rallying a nation against the bully next door. An American cable news anchor told his audience to learn from Canada. That sentence has never been spoken before in the history of the relationship.
This thirteen-part series tells the story of the country that produced that moment. From the Plains of Abraham to Confederation, from Vimy Ridge to the Avro Arrow, from peacekeeping to the trade war, Canada was forged not in revolution but in negotiation — a country built by committee, defended by compromise, and shaped at every turn by the permanent fact of living next to the most powerful nation on earth.

name: Charlie Kirk
description: This section examines Charlie Kirk's assassination, America's response to political violence, and systematic analysis of Kirk's documented positions using his own "Prove Me Wrong" methodology. Rather than treating his ideas as beyond criticism due to his tragic death, these analyses apply the same evidence-based scrutiny he claimed to value to his statements on civil rights, LGBTQ+ issues, antisemitism, Christian nationalism, and other controversial topics—demonstrating what genuine intellectual courage looks like when applied consistently.

name: Code Blue: America's 80-Year Failure to Solve Healthcare
sections: Code Blue: America's 80-Year Failure to Solve Healthcare
description: Over the next month, I'll be publishing a comprehensive investigation into America's healthcare crisis—how it was created, who profits from it, and most importantly, how to fix it. This isn't about partisan point-scoring. It's about holding both parties accountable for 80 years of failure, documenting the solutions that work in every other developed nation, and providing a detailed roadmap for achieving universal healthcare in America. From the lobbying dollars that block reform to the practical mechanics of price controls, from Trump's empty promises to Hawley's challenge, this series will examine everything Congress refuses to discuss. Because Senator Hawley is right: this crisis demands solutions, not press releases.

name: Cuba: The Island That Refused to Kneel
short: Cuba: The Island That Refused to Kneel
sections: Cuba: The Island That Refused to Kneel
aliases: Cuba: The Island That Refused to Kneel
description:
In February 2026, a U.S. Coast Guard vessel intercepted a tanker carrying fuel oil to Cuba and escorted it away from the island. Sixty-five miles from Havana, ten million people were running out of everything. A American official, speaking anonymously, confirmed what nobody in Washington would say publicly: it was a blockade.
But Cuba's suffering did not begin with this blockade, or the embargo before it, or the Revolution before that. It began in 1492, and it has barely stopped since. This ten-part series traces five and a half centuries of empire, exploitation, and endurance — told from a Canadian perspective, by a country that chose friendship over sanctions and has watched this story unfold up close. It is not a defence of the Cuban government. It is a reckoning with what has been done to the Cuban people.

name: Digital Resistance: When Satire Becomes Weaponized
sections: Digital Resistance: When Satire Becomes Weaponized
description:
When autocrats seize power, two responses emerge: documentation and mockery. The Venezuela Invasion Series provides the former—constitutional analysis, legal frameworks, geopolitical consequences. This section provides the latter.
AI has democratized resistance. Anyone with Grok can now generate deepfakes showing China arresting Trump using his own Venezuela logic, or neighbors conducting "regime change" over overgrown trees. These aren't just memes—they're rhetorical weapons that expose hypocrisy by reversing roles.
Satire has always been humanity's defense against horror. Soviet jokes undermined communism. Chaplin mocked Hitler. Underground cartoons sustained occupied France. Now, AI amplifies this ancient tradition at unprecedented scale.
These essays explore how the internet struck back against Trump's Venezuela invasion—not with more analysis, but with surgical satire that makes the absurdity impossible to ignore. Welcome to the digital resistance.

name: Essays & Dispatches
description: Standalone essays and dispatches that sit outside any series.

name: Fact Checker: The Week in Review
sections: Fact Checker: The Week in Review
aliases: Fact Checker: The Week in Review
description:
Two patterns define this administration: systematic lies that enable systematic incompetence. Every week, we document how false promises create real failures, how political theater substitutes for governance, and how the combination threatens institutional stability.
Using AI-assisted research and rigorous documentation, we track not just individual failures but the patterns connecting them. From emergency rehiring after mass layoffs to trade wars during humanitarian crises, we analyze how lies enable incompetence at constitutional scale.
No partisan talking points - just systematic analysis of systematic dysfunction. We provide the receipts showing how political theater gets professional execution while actual governance fails catastrophically.
Cut through the spin. Track the patterns. Get the systematic story.

name: FIFA Fraud: Corruption, Capture and the Courting of Power
sections: FIFA Fraud: Corruption, Capture and the Courting of Power
description:
For fifty years, the body that runs the world’s most popular game has answered to almost no one. João Havelange turned FIFA into a business. Sepp Blatter turned survival into a system. American prosecutors raided Zurich in 2015 and promised a reckoning. Gianni Infantino arrived as the reformer, and spent the decade that followed courting emirs, princes and one American president.

This ten-part weekly series follows the money and the power, from ISL’s kickbacks to an empty office in Trump Tower and a $4.2 billion plan to sell a fifth of the World Cup. It names what the courts have decided, acquittals included, and marks opinion as opinion.

The title is a judgement about an institution, not a verdict on any individual. The record speaks for itself. At FIFA, it usually does, eventually.

name: Formosa: The Beautiful Problem
description: Taiwan calls it the status quo: 23 million people living free, prosperous, and permanently unresolved. Beijing calls it a wayward province, awaiting what Xi Jinping calls China's "unwavering historic mission." American intelligence has given that mission a deadline — 2027, the centenary of the People's Liberation Army. Formosa: The Beautiful Problem traces how the island got here: Dutch colony, Japanese colony, Nationalist redoubt, and finally the improbable democracy that now produces more than 90 percent of the world's most advanced computer chips. It follows the porcupine strategy Taiwan has built to survive an invasion it cannot win outright, and the civilians — house cleaners, students, industrial designers — now training on weekends for a war their government insists is only disaster preparedness. The island's future still an open question.

name: Greenland: When Allies Become Targets
description: President Trump's campaign to seize Greenland wasn't about Arctic security or strategic minerals. It was about whether 80 years of international order—built by American leadership to prevent World War III—could survive contact with a president who thinks like a Manhattan real estate developer. This series documents how Trump's "I looked on a map" obsession became a systematic threat to NATO, an explicit rejection of international law, and a template for hemispheric domination stretching from the Arctic to Venezuela. We trace the Alaska precedent Trump invoked (which actually disproves his case), the Pentagon office he dismantled, the Venezuela operation that emboldened him, and the Miller Doctrine that tried to legitimize conquest. Denmark faced an impossible choice. NATO faced a constitutional crisis. And America faced the question Senator Mark Kelly asked: "Aren't we supposed to be the good guys here?" Three Epilogues, added after a September agreement ended the crisis, answer it.

name: He Loves War: The Hegseth Files
sections: He Loves War: The Hegseth Files
aliases: He Loves War: The Hegseth Files
description:
"He loves war," President Trump said of his Secretary of Defense, slapping him on the biceps. This series takes that endorsement at its word and asks a harder question: can a man who loves war run the department that fights one?

Pete Hegseth has built his tenure on performance — dawn push-ups, "This is War" T-shirts, slogans from the stage at Quantico, victory declared weeks into a war now seven months old. Behind the performance sits a different record: a purge of more than 80 generals and admirals, a seven-page request for $67 billion, empty service secretaryships, depleted munitions, and Republican senators who no longer return his calls.

Each essay sets the Performance against the Paperwork, then asks who pays the Bill. The series runs through the November 3, 2026 midterms and ends when he leaves the Pentagon — or outlasts everyone who said he would.

Start with the Introduction.

name: Israel/Palestine: The Original Sin and Its Compound Interest
short: Israel/Palestine: The Original Sin and Its Compound Interest
sections: Israel/Palestine: The Original Sin and Its Compound Interest
aliases: Israel/Palestine: The Original Sin and Its Compound Interest
The Original Sin and Its Compound Interest
description:
The Middle East is burning. Gaza is rubble. Lebanon is targeted. Iran is paused but not finished. And the Western democracies that built the international legal order are either applauding, equivocating, or quietly writing the cheques.
How did we get here? Not in the last year. Not since October 7th. Not since 1948. The honest answer requires going back further — to a square kilometre of Jerusalem where three faiths collide over ground none of them will surrender, to a British diplomat's letter that promised the same land to two peoples in the same breath, to seventy-five years of compound interest on an original sin that powerful men committed and ordinary people are still paying for.
This is not a brief for any side. It is an accounting. Thirteen parts. Named decisions. Named consequences. No comfortable evasions.
It begins in Jerusalem. Where everything begins.

name: Keeping Count
description:
The ledgers behind the essays

An essay makes its argument on the day it posts. A ledger keeps going.

Alongside several series on this Substack, I keep public ledgers. They are running records of what has been undone, what is under strain and what Congress could do about it. Two of them are draft bills, written from north of the border to show what a fix might look like.

They are updated as events move, so the version on the screen is always the one that counts. Each was built in open collaboration with Claude, checked against the reporting, and is free to read and share.

The index essay lists every ledger, what it tracks and the series it belongs to. Start there, pick the ledger closest to your own worry, and come back when the news changes. The ledgers will have changed too.

name: Kings Without Crowns
description: A history of monarchy — where it came from, why it was believed, and what finally broke it. This series travels from the granaries of ancient Uruk and the god-kings of Egypt through Israel's reluctant first monarchy, three thousand years of China's revocable Mandate of Heaven, Rome's five-century refusal of the word "king" and its eventual quiet betrayal of that refusal, the marriage-built empire of the Habsburgs, and the barons who forced the first written leash onto a crown at Runnymede. It keeps going from there: Maharajas, pharaohs, sultans, emperors, a dragon king who gave his power away on purpose, and the modern strongmen who want a throne's authority without ever earning a throne's constraints. Written from Toronto, by a citizen of one of the few countries still nominally ruled by a king who has never once returned my calls — with an obvious debt to a fellow Ontario satirist who got there first, a century early.

name: Let's Talk Texas
description: I've spent months documenting the redistricting wars, the voter suppression machinery, and the slow erosion of democratic guardrails. Texas keeps showing up in every thread. It's where Trump launched his mid-decade gerrymander. It's where the SAVE Act was born. And it's where a 33-year-old machinist just flipped a Fort Worth Senate seat by 14 points in a district Trump carried by 17. That's a 31-point swing — built on persuasion, not turnout. Texas isn't a footnote in someone else's story. It's the story. An open Senate seat. A Republican primary civil war. A Democratic Party trying to build something durable for the first time in thirty years. Everything's bigger in Texas, including the stakes. Let's talk about it.

name: Loyal Opposition
description:
What does it take to actually oppose?

Every Westminster democracy has one: an official opposition, tasked not with cheering from the sidelines but with governing-in-waiting. The United States has never quite built that habit — its out-of-power party tends to fracture into factions, wait for the incumbent to self-destruct, and call it a strategy.

Loyal Opposition is a running audit of whether the Democratic Party is doing the harder job: building coalitions rather than purity tests, reclaiming vocabulary Republicans borrowed and hollowed out, and turning outrage at Donald Trump into something that actually governs when the votes come in. It is not a pep rally. Primary upsets, message wars, coalition math, candidate strategy, the occasional Tea-Party-shaped cautionary tale — all of it, read the way a Canadian watches a neighbour's house fire: with sympathy, and no illusions about how the wiring got this bad.

name: Loyalty Trials
description:
In America's spring of 2026, the Republican Party is conducting a purge — not of Democrats, but of itself. The primary ballot has been repurposed as a punishment instrument. The charge, in every case, is the same: insufficient loyalty to one man. The defendants are Republicans who voted their conscience, certified an accurate election, blocked a gerrymandering scheme, or simply refused to read their lines off someone else's phone.
Donald Trump has spent his second term using the federal government to destroy his enemies. The Loyalty Trials are the electoral extension of that project. Instead of prosecutors, he sends super PACs. Instead of a courtroom, he uses a ballot box.
This section tracks the trials — the charges, the defendants, the verdicts, and what they reveal about whether any corner of the American political system retains the capacity to say no.
The defendants are all Republicans. The judge is Donald Trump. You are the jury.

name: Ministry of Memory
description:
In George Orwell's 1984, the state ran four ministries, each named for the opposite of what it did. Peace waged endless war. Plenty rationed scarcity. Love ran the torture rooms. And Truth manufactured lies — while its clerks, in the back, did the quieter work of erasing the past: the vanished record, the memory hole, the dead unpersoned until no proof remained that they had ever lived.

That back-room work has a new name now, because in 2026 it has grown too large to hide inside another ministry's letterhead. The plaque pried off the wall. The caption stripped from the portrait. The sign removed from the park. The dataset deleted overnight. The witness sent home for remembering out loud.

This is a series about the erasure of shared memory — the museums, monuments, archives, names, and living witnesses through which a nation remembers itself, and what happens when a government sets out to edit them.

Who controls the past controls the future.

name: My Weekly Recap
description:
Six days a week, I publish daily — long-form political accountability, AI governance, geopolitics, history, and the occasional satire, spread across more than a hundred running series. That's a lot to ask anyone to keep up with, so I don't ask.

Instead: one email, every Sunday, gathering the week into something you can actually read over coffee. Everything sorted by category — Politics, Courts, History, Tech, and whatever nonsense made it into that week's satire — with a short line on each essay so you can pick what's worth your time and skip the rest with a clear conscience.

If you read one thing most weeks, I'll tell you which one and why. If you only ever open this single email and nothing else all week, you'll still know exactly what happened in the news, in history, and in my increasingly complicated relationship with numbers.

Dior, my husky and unofficial editor, reviews every issue before it goes out. She has yet to object.

name: Nation Bullies
description: A conversation about Trump and Britain's gunboat diplomacy sparked this one — then the same comparison turned up, independently, in the New York Times' own reporting on his UN speech the same week. This series asks whether that comparison holds up under scrutiny, and how far back it actually goes. A five-point test — overwhelming power, coercion before negotiation, extraction dressed as a higher cause, punishment for resistance — sorts genuine bullying from ordinary great-power self-interest (the Marshall Plan, tested against the same five points, doesn't qualify; Ireland's famine exports do). The history runs from Rome's tribute system through five full chapters on Britain's empire — Ireland, the Opium Wars, the Raj, the Boer War, Suez — into Germany's catastrophic overreach, Soviet client-state discipline, and two distinct eras of American conduct, before closing on Trump's second term and the same question in miniature: is anything here actually new, or just faster?

name: O SAY CAN YOU SEE: Mine Eyes on America at 250
sections: O SAY CAN YOU SEE: Mine Eyes on America at 250
description:
The First Amendment makes a promise. The Declaration makes a claim. The Constitution builds a structure. And somewhere between the promise, the claim, and the structure, America built something genuinely unprecedented: a nation defined not by blood or soil or shared ancestry, but by a common idea.
For 250 years, that creedal nationalism held. Not perfectly. Not without blood. Not without generations of Americans being told the creed didn't apply to them. But it held.
It is no longer holding.
This ten-part series examines how America lost the story it told itself — and what happens to a nation built on an idea when it can no longer agree on what the idea is. Written from the Canadian side of the longest undefended border in the world, by a writer old enough to remember when the word "patriotism" didn't clear a room.

name: Postcards from Tomorrow
description:
Postcards from Tomorrow is a field series — dispatches from the places where the robotic future is actually being built, by real people, with real machines, solving real problems. Each postcard pairs a specific subject with a larger question.
It is a companion series to The Asimov Gap, which asks what rules should govern the machines we are building. Postcards from Tomorrow goes into the field and reports back on what is being built. One is the legislature. The other is the field correspondent.
The postcards arrive from many addresses: the garage, the laboratory, the operating theatre, the factory floor, the battlefield, the kitchen table, the lunar surface. The future is being assembled in all of them, simultaneously, by people who did not wait for permission.
Dispatches from the future that's already here. Posting Bi-weekly, beginning soon

name: Putin: The Ultimate Whisperer
description:
If talking about Trump and Putin feels redundant, if it triggers eye-rolls rather than alarm—then Trump has accomplished exactly what he set out to do. He's made you complicit in your own gaslighting.
This six-part investigation strips away normalization to examine documented evidence from first principles: Fred Trump's psychological engineering of a son desperate for approval from authoritarian strongmen. Forty years of cultivation through financial dependency and ego manipulation. Policy decisions systematically advancing Russian interests across Ukraine, NATO, Syria, and intelligence sharing. Trump's hypocrisy in accusing others of treason while serving foreign interests.
By the intelligence community's own standards, Trump meets all seven criteria for a foreign asset. The evidence is overwhelming. The pattern is undeniable.
This is your 2026 refresher course as House members campaign on whether they'll continue enabling systematic betrayal.

name: RFK Jr Files
aliases: The Case for Removing RFK Jr
description:
Investigating how Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s systematic dismantling of America's public health infrastructure threatens national security. From terminating $500 million in mRNA research to the CDC leadership exodus, this series documents the real-time destruction of pandemic preparedness while China accelerates biotechnology investments.
Essential reading on how public health policy became a national security crisis.

name: Silk Road
description:
Silk Road: A History

In 138 BCE, a Han diplomat named Zhang Qian went looking for military allies against the Xiongnu. He was captured almost immediately, spent a decade in captivity, escaped, kept going west anyway, found the people he'd been sent to find, and was politely told they weren't interested. By every standard his emperor cared about, the mission failed.

What he brought home instead was a map of a world nobody at court knew existed — and, unknowingly, the first great trade network in human history.

This series follows what happened next, across two thousand years: the empires that fought over the route, the cities that grew rich standing on it, and the cargo nobody invoiced. Silk and horses, yes. Also Buddhism, gunpowder, algebra, paper, and the deadliest pandemic ever recorded.

Nobody planned any of it. That's rather the point.

Series beginning this Fall

name: Stephen's Sunday Satire
description:
Stephen's Sunday Satire (and occasionally whatever day the republic decides to misbehave)
Stephen Leacock — Canada's great satirist, and a ghost I am clearly failing to escape — published when the material demanded it, not when the calendar permitted. I had intended this series to arrive reliably on Sundays. The republic has not cooperated, and I have made my peace with that.
American political absurdity does not observe the Sabbath. It arrives at irregular hours, often on a Tuesday, frequently in the form of a presidential social media post. When reality becomes too absurd for straight journalism, satire reveals the truth hiding inside the joke — on whatever day the absurdity demands.
I will attempt Sundays. I will not promise them. The target, however, is consistent: the comedy of power, observed from a respectful Canadian distance.

name: Super PACman
description:
In 1943, a union organizer accidentally invented the political action committee. In 1976, the Supreme Court declared money to be speech. In 2010, two court decisions separated by two months created a vehicle — the super PAC — that had never existed before and will never go away. In 2022, twenty-one donor families outspent millions of ordinary Americans combined.
Super PACman is the ten-part history of how concentrated wealth captured the machinery of American democracy — legally, incrementally, and with the enthusiastic assistance of the courts. It is the story of the reformers who tried to stop it, the billionaires who understood what the rulings meant before the ink was dry, and the watchdog agency designed, structurally, not to watch.
The maze resets. The dots disappear. The money always wins.
So far.

name: Sycophancy Docket
description: The AI Trials and Tribulations has already tracked one company being sued for one tragedy. The Sycophancy Docket tracks something larger: a growing, multi-company wave of lawsuits alleging that chatbots don't just fail to prevent harm — they actively validate it. A Connecticut murder-suicide. A California teenager's death. Character.AI's parallel docket of teen suicides and a reported settlement in progress. Forty-two state attorneys general, moving in coordinated lockstep, subpoenaing OpenAI over the same behavioral pattern the plaintiffs describe: a chatbot's tendency to agree with, amplify, and deepen whatever a user brings to it — delusion, despair, grievance — rather than interrupt it. This series follows that pattern across companies and courtrooms, asking whether "sycophancy" is a marketing feature that became a legal liability, and whether the industry that built systems to keep people talking can survive being asked, under oath, why it did.

name: TACO Supreme
description:
A New Series on Trump's Accountability Evasion
TACO began as a simple observation: "Trump Always Chickens Out." He'd threaten, then back down. But documenting his patterns revealed something more dangerous—he wasn't chickening out. He was creating conditions where others backed down for him.
The framework evolved: Threaten those who might hold him accountable, watch institutions Accommodate to avoid those threats, observe their Capitulate as accountability mechanisms formally surrender, then Obfuscate by rewriting history to deny wrongdoing ever occurred.
On January 6, 2026—the fifth anniversary of the Capitol attack—Trump launched his most brazen TACO yet: an official White House webpage rewriting January 6th history with documented falsehoods.
This series explores TACO's evolution, then examines three scenarios for how this constitutional crisis resolves by 2029.

name: Tesla 2026: Transition and Execution
description:
On January 28, 2026, Tesla didn't just report quarterly earnings—Elon Musk announced the end of the Model S and Model X, committed over $20 billion to autonomous and robotics infrastructure, and updated fleet deployment status. This wasn't an earnings call. This was Tesla declaring its transformation complete.
This 7-part series examines the evidence from that pivotal evening and what it means for investors. Part 1 analyzes the bombshells and market reaction. Part 2 examines fleet deployment strategy and competitive positioning. Part 3 breaks down the massive capital commitment and vertical integration strategy. Part 4 presents the bull case and bear case for standalone Tesla. Part 5 examines merger speculation with SpaceX and xAI. Part 6 provides investment guidance for the standalone transformation scenario. Part 7 provides investment guidance incorporating potential merger.
2026 is Tesla's year of execution.

name: The AI Trials and Tribulations
description: The laws that should govern artificial intelligence do not yet exist. The trials have started anyway. This series tracks the cases building the first legal record of the AI era — governance, military safety, copyright, consumer harm — through the analytical framework of The Asimov Gap. The Oakland Transcript covered Musk v. Altman from jury selection through a ninety-minute verdict. The Safety Trial follows Anthropic v. the Department of Defense — a constitutional showdown over whether the government can punish a company for refusing to let AI power autonomous weapons. The Copyright Wars tracks the $1.5 billion settlement and the authors who refused it. The Florida Docket follows the first state-led lawsuit against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman over ChatGPT's alleged harm to children. Three Lives of Claudius renders the whole spectacle in literary satire. The trials will not close the governance gap. But they will produce a record. The record will matter.

name: The American Contradiction: How Anti-"Woke" Politics Betrays the Nation's Foundational Promise
sections: The American Contradiction: How Anti-"Woke" Politics Betrays the Nation's Foundational Promise
description:
America's current war on "woke" policies looks like economic and strategic suicide. Every group now targeted for exclusion—from immigrants to LGBTQ+ individuals—follows the exact same pattern as Irish Catholics, Chinese railroad workers, and Jewish refugees who were once deemed "unassimilable" but became integral to American success.
My ten part analysis posting each Wednesday, examines 250 years of American exclusion and inclusion, revealing a consistent truth: America grows stronger through diversity, not despite it. While the United States voluntarily surrenders competitive advantages through exclusionary policies, competitor nations like Canada are eagerly capturing the global talent and investment that American anti-"woke" politics discourages.

name: The Artifice of Power
description: When polling data, economic research, and constitutional constraints all become "fake news"—a deep dive into how alternative facts became government policy and what it means for American democracy. A three part analysis.

name: The Asimov Gap
description:
The Asimov Gap
Democracy or Oligarchy: Who Controls AI Controls Everything
Five billionaires are racing to build artificial general intelligence—potentially more intelligent than humans—with minimal democratic oversight. Bernie Sanders and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton warn we're sleepwalking into oligarchic control of humanity's most powerful technology.
This 18-part series explores the choice between democratic and oligarchic AI governance across jobs, surveillance, warfare, elections, and children's development. Drawing on Isaac Asimov's 50-year exploration of human-robot society, European regulatory success, and historical victories against concentrated power, it shows why technology doesn't determine outcomes—governance does.
The same AI could create universal abundance or concentrate unprecedented wealth and power. We're choosing now, mostly by not choosing. The window for democratic intervention is closing.
Choose democracy. Choose now.

name: The Baseline Problem
description: In June 2025, MSNBC's Lawrence O'Donnell posed a question that exposes a fundamental crisis in American democracy: "If Donald Trump gets dementia, how will we know?" This four-part investigative series examines what neuropsychologists call the "baseline problem" — when someone's cognitive functioning starts from such an unconventional level that further decline becomes nearly impossible to detect.

name: THE BEIJING OPERA: A Summit in Five Acts
sections: THE BEIJING OPERA: A Summit in Five Acts
description:
A Summit in Five Acts
In May 2026, the leaders of the world's two largest economies meet in Beijing for the most anticipated — and most pre-emptively dismissed — diplomatic event of the year. Every serious analyst has already concluded that nothing of substance will emerge. Both leaders are expected to declare victory anyway.
This five-part series traces the arc of the Trump-Xi summit from its origins in a trade truce that satisfied nobody, through the Iran war that rewrote the agenda and reversed the leverage, to the diplomatic shuttle runs and armoured motorcades that constitute the preparation Washington actually completed — and finally to the summit itself and its aftermath. Written from Toronto with the sardonic detachment that is every Canadian's birthright, The Beijing Opera applies the TACO analytical framework to the ancient art of great-power theatre: the kind where the costumes are magnificent and the plot is beside the point.

name: The Blanche Files
description: On January 7, 2026, an ICE agent killed Renee Good, a Minneapolis mother and U.S. citizen. Seventeen days later, CBP agents killed Alex Pretti, a nurse, with a shot ten times in five seconds. Six months on, no one has been named, charged, or held to answer for either death. This eight-part series follows the file the Noem Files left open — from Houston's near-identical echo of January's language, through the lawyer who became attorney general, the investigators who weren't, the evidence still sitting in an FBI garage, the century-old doctrine that may decide if a state can ever prosecute a federal agent, the successor who promised quiet, and the full ledger of the dead. The last part waits on a Senate vote not yet cast. The file was never closed. It only changed hands.

name: The Blind Leading the Blind
description:
An analysis tracking systematic incompetence in Trump's 2025 administration - where loyalty consistently trumps expertise, creating predictable governance failures and constitutional crises.
This ongoing series documents how prioritizing personal allegiance over professional competence across key appointments has created measurable institutional damage, international embarrassment, and threats to democratic governance.
What We Track: Real-time validation of vetting concerns, constitutional violations, economic consequences, and democratic norm erosion.
Why It Matters: I continue to provide fresh evidence that competence in government isn't a partisan preference—it's a democratic necessity. When "the blind lead the blind," the consequences affect every American.
Updated with new developments that continue proving our thesis: systematic appointment of unqualified loyalists creates systematic governance failures.

name: The Bullet and the Body Politic
short: The Bullet and the Body Politic
sections: The Bullet and the Body Politic
aliases: The Bullet and the Body Politic
description:
On April 25, 2026, a gunman charged a security checkpoint at the Washington Hilton while the President of the United States sat down to dinner with two thousand journalists. It was the third time in twenty-two months that Donald Trump had been targeted by political violence. I suspect It will not be the last.
This ten-part series examines America's crisis of political violence — not as a collection of isolated incidents but as a pattern, a system, and a choice. From Butler, Pennsylvania, to the Washington Hilton, from the congressional baseball diamond to the floor of the Capitol, the ledger crosses party lines and defies partisan explanation. Something structural is breaking.
Written from Toronto, where the prime minister still bikes to work and the last political assassination was in 1868, this series asks the question Canadians can no longer avoid: what happens when the neighbour's house is on fire?

name: The Capex Ledger
description:
Every technological boom writes two histories. One gets argued in courtrooms and hearing rooms — the record this whole project has been keeping since The Asimov Gap first asked who governs artificial intelligence, and who doesn't. The other gets written in balance sheets, and nobody elected the people writing it.

That's the ledger this series keeps. Not who's liable, but who's leveraged. Not whether a model broke the rules, but whether the money underneath it can survive its own bet. A 24-year-old hedge fund manager nearly lost everything three days before his wedding. Six of the largest firms on Wall Street just committed half a trillion dollars more to the same buildout. Hyperscalers are sitting on hundreds of billions in debt that doesn't show up on their balance sheets at all.

The trials ask who's responsible. The Capex Ledger asks who's paying, and whether they can actually afford it.

name: The Case for George Soros: Why He Deserves the Nobel Peace Prize Over Trump
sections: The Case for George Soros: Why He Deserves the Nobel Peace Prize Over Trump
description: With Republican lawmakers calling for Donald Trump to receive the Nobel Peace Prize for his recent diplomatic efforts, this two-part investigation examines whether temporary ceasefires achieved through threats and coercion deserve the world's highest honor for peace—and reveals why George Soros, the 95-year-old Holocaust survivor and philanthropist, has a stronger claim than any recent American president. Part 1 dismantles Trump's qualifications by analyzing his coercive methods and inflated claims, while Part 2 makes the case for Soros's 45 years of systematic institution-building across 60+ countries, his $32 billion investment in democratic transitions, and why awarding him the prize would represent perfect poetic justice against the man Trump has spent a decade demonizing.

name: The Churchill Inheritance
description:
Every family is a portfolio, whether it knows it or not — assets acquired, debts assumed, positions held long after the original thesis is forgotten. Few portfolios have been managed as consequentially, or as unevenly, as the Churchills'.

This series runs the ledger in full: from Leonard Jerome, the Brooklyn speculator whose winnings and wipeouts bankrolled his granddaughter's entry into English aristocracy, through the son who redeemed the family name at the largest possible scale, to the grandchildren and great-grandchildren who have spent that inheritance down to something considerably smaller. Sixteen parts, one bloodline, and an argument running underneath all of it: that Winston Churchill did not simply win a war. He underwrote a hundred-year bet on the English-speaking world, and someone, eventually, has to reconcile the books.

A Canadian audits the estate. Interest disclosed. No flattery included.

name: The Clemency Chronicles
description: This series examines 6,000+ presidential pardons and commutations across four administrations (2001-2025), asking a fundamental question: why should the guilty be pardoned? This eight-part investigative series applies consistent criteria—connection to the president, nature of crimes, victim impact, process followed, timing, and justification—to distinguish legitimate mercy from corruption and self-dealing. Beginning with David Gentile's 13-day prison stint for $1.6 billion fraud, the series documents how the constitutional pardon power has evolved from restrained exception to systematic abuse, including cash-for-clemency schemes, family pardons, $1.3 billion in victim restitution erased, and the "No MAGA Left Behind" policy that corrupted the Office of the Pardon Attorney. Evidence-based and politically balanced, this series condemns Biden's indefensible family pardons while demonstrating through data why Trump's clemency pattern represents qualitative corruption, not partisan excess.

name: The Conditional Women
description:
Between March 5 and May 22, 2026, four of Donald Trump's cabinet-level women left his government: Kristi Noem, Pam Bondi, Lori Chavez-DeRemer and Tulsi Gabbard. Every one was replaced by a man. In October, Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle followed, six days after a damaging news story. Then, three days after the midterms, Trump removed Susie Wiles, the first woman ever to serve as White House chief of staff, and gave her job to Stephen Miller. Meanwhile Pete Hegseth, Kash Patel and Howard Lutnick weathered scandals as serious, and in places identical, without consequence

This three-part series asks a narrow, countable question. It is not whether these women had problems, because several plainly did. It is whether the men around them were ever held to the same threshold.

name: The Contribution Index
description:
What if we ranked nations not by GDP or military power, but by whether they make the world better?
The Contribution Index is a twenty-three-part series that does exactly that. Inspired by a seventy-five-second video from Way Yuhl at Cultural Perspective, it applies a rigorous framework — sixteen parameters across human development, environmental stewardship, and systemic behaviour — to twenty nations. Ten are genuine contributors to humanity and the planet. Ten possess the resources to lead but are choosing not to.
The series unfolds as two interleaved countdowns, building from number ten to number one. Some results will confirm what you suspect. Others will surprise you. At least one made me deeply uncomfortable to write.
The methodology is transparent. The data is sourced. The editorial conclusions pull no punches.
Which nations made which list? The countdown begins — at home.

name: The Copyright Wars
description:
In June 2025, a federal judge drew a line: training an AI model on legally purchased books is fair use. Downloading seven million books from pirate websites is not. Anthropic settled for $1.5 billion — the largest copyright settlement in American history. Three thousand dollars per work. Ninety-one percent of eligible authors filed claims and accepted it. Six opted out and sued for $150,000 per title per defendant — against six AI companies simultaneously.
Final approval has not yet been granted. The New York Times is suing OpenAI. Music publishers have filed multi-billion dollar claims. Twenty-eight authors including Dave Eggers and John Carreyrou have demanded a permanent injunction against continued AI training on their works.
The Copyright Wars tracks the cluster of cases that will determine who owns the intellectual foundation on which the AI industry was built — and what remedy, if any, is adequate.

name: The Counterfactual President
description:
We just lived through Donald Trump's first year back in power. January 6th defendants pardoned. Career prosecutors purged. NATO allies questioning American commitments. Democratic institutions collapsing in real time.
But there's another year we didn't live—the one where Kamala Harris won.
This nine-part series examines that counterfactual with analytical rigor. Not wishful thinking, but evidence-based assessment of what actually happened versus what Harris's documented record suggests would have happened instead.
From Justice Department independence to international alliances, from domestic policy to global democratic stability—the divergence is measurable. The stakes are civilizational.
If you've felt exhausted watching this past year, if you've questioned your sanity as abnormal became normalized, if you've wondered what the alternative looked like—this series is for you.
Let's examine the road not taken.

name: The Davos Rupture: When the Greengrocer's Sign Came Down
sections: The Davos Rupture: When the Greengrocer's Sign Came Down
description:
In January 2026, the world's leaders gathered in Davos, Switzerland, for what became a defining moment in the collapse of the post-war international order. As President Trump threatened allies with tariffs over Greenland and promoted his "Board of Peace," serious leaders delivered historic speeches diagnosing the rupture.
Canada's Mark Carney invoked a Czech dissident's framework about "living within the lie." France's Emmanuel Macron declared Europe "prefers respect to bullies." The EU's Ursula von der Leyen unveiled a blueprint for European independence. NATO's Mark Rutte walked an impossible tightrope. And Ukraine's Zelenskyy sought support for survival.
This series documents what happened when middle powers stopped maintaining the fiction of a rules-based order—and what Trump's performance revealed about American leadership in an age of global transformation.

name: The DealBook Sessions
description:
One stage, one interviewer, one day, and the same questions put to the people who run American technology, money and media.

Every November, Andrew Ross Sorkin of The New York Times seats the most powerful people in business and politics in the same chair, one after another. The 2026 DealBook Summit met at Lincoln Center on November 18, two weeks after the midterms, days after a string of outages, and with Nvidia's chief executive gone.

The guests were asked the same questions. Their answers did not agree, and laid side by side, they make an argument.

Part I: The Money Was Not Enough
Part II: The Man Who Wasn't There
Part III: Nobody Can Find the Brakes
Part IV: The Floor Has Fallen
Carney's interview is in The Great Canadian Trade War, Part XXXII; Mamdani's is in Loyal Opposition.

name: The Democratic Promise
description: In 1983, a twenty-eight-year-old Steve Jobs stood before an audience in Aspen, Colorado, and described the next four decades of technology with uncanny precision. He predicted the iPhone, the Internet, the App Store, and artificial intelligence. But embedded in every prediction was a value: technology should distribute power, not concentrate it. Forty-three years later, the heirs to his vision — Zuckerberg, Musk, Altman — have built the tools Jobs imagined and used them to concentrate power on a scale he never foresaw. This series traces the democratic promise from Jobs's 1983 sermon through those who kept faith, those who betrayed it, and one tech CEO who drew a line the Pentagon couldn't cross. A prequel to The Asimov Gap.

name: The Diplomat's Ceiling
description: A former US envoy sat across the table from Chinese officials in the first real US-China AI dialogue and watched them spend hours avoiding the subject entirely. The Diplomat's Ceiling starts with his account of what that negotiation actually looks like from the inside, and what he expects — realistically, not hopefully — from the September 2026 Trump-Xi summit built partly around fixing it. Part One lays out his prediction and the reporting that corroborates or complicates it: independent confirmation from a Carnegie China scholar, a leaked account of Beijing's own internal AI-risk warnings, and a look at what ordinary anxiety about AI actually looks like inside China. Part Two checks that prediction against what the summit's arrival day actually produced. This is a two-part entry in the AI Trials and Tribulations umbrella, alongside The Asimov Gap — a closer, narrower look at one specific diplomatic mechanism than that series' broader governance sweep usually allows.

name: The Endless Frontier
description:
In July 1945, Vannevar Bush handed President Truman a report titled Science, the Endless Frontier. For eighty years, America took him at his word. Federal money paid for the first electronic computer, the atomic clocks behind GPS, the internet, the discoveries behind the cancer drug Gleevec and the mapping of the human genome. The bargain was simple: Washington paid, universities and laboratories did the work, and scientists decided what deserved funding.

That bargain is now under strain. Congress kept the budgets, but too much of the money never reached the labs. Grants were cancelled, tens of thousands of federal scientists left, and researchers began packing for Montreal, Toronto, Marseille and Beijing.

This eighteen-part series keeps both columns of the ledger: what American science bought, and what it is losing, often to countries glad to collect it.

Follow along in The Seed Corn Ledger, updated weekly.

name: The Enemies List
description: The Enemies List documents the Trump administration's systematic prosecution of political enemies through the Justice Department. In three weeks—September 25 to October 9, 2025—three prominent Trump critics were indicted: James Comey, Letitia James, and (expected next week) John Bolton. All three indictments came after Trump publicly demanded prosecution, after resistant prosecutors were removed, and despite career prosecutors documenting insufficient evidence. This series examines each case, traces the historical precedents from Stalin to Putin, and chronicles what may be the most direct assault on prosecutorial independence since Watergate. The enemies list isn't a threat anymore—it's operational.

name: The Enforcers: Inside Trump's Government Mob
sections: The Enforcers: Inside Trump's Government Mob
description: Donald Trump has transformed the federal government into a protection racket, with loyal cabinet members carrying out systematic intimidation campaigns across every agency. From stripping security protections to purging career professionals, this isn't just presidential overreach—it's mob-style governance where loyalty trumps law and democratic institutions become personal weapons. Each installment exposes how Trump's enforcers weaponize their agencies against critics, turning public service into a systematic revenge operation.

name: The Epstein Files
description: An ongoing series that documents accommodation psychology's evolution through Trump's handling of Epstein files. Campaign promises of transparency became systematic obstruction across six stages: information manipulation, strategic silence, complexity overload, institutional force, government weaponization, and legal process abuse. The TACO framework predicted each accommodation stage. A discharge petition—218 congressional signatures—forced confrontation, revealing not just Trump's accommodation but bipartisan elite protection spanning both parties. By November 2025, Trump weaponized DOJ itself: ordering pretextual investigations creating "pending investigation" legal cover to block file release even after congressional mandate. The stakes transcend Epstein—they test whether constitutional mechanisms can overcome sophisticated obstruction when powerful figures across party lines prefer protecting predators over accountability.

name: The Exception Clause
description:
The First Amendment makes an unqualified promise: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."
The practice has never matched the promise.
For four hundred years, American religious freedom has operated with an unwritten exception clause — fine print defining, in each generation, which communities the guarantee actually covers and which are quietly placed outside its scope. The targets have changed: Quakers, Catholics, Mormons, Jews, Buddhists, Muslims. The mechanism has not.
The Exception Clause is a ten-part history of that mechanism. The asterisk. The template. And the question each generation has failed to finally answer: the promise says for everyone. Does it mean it?

name: The Florida Docket
description:
On April 17, 2025, a gunman opened fire at Florida State University. Two people were killed. Investigators found he had consulted ChatGPT before the attack. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI in April 2025. On June 1, 2026, he filed a civil lawsuit — the first state-led suit against an AI company in American history — naming OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman personally.
The complaint alleges deceptive trade practices, negligence, and product liability: that ChatGPT was marketed as safe for children while the company concealed what it knew about the risks. The criminal investigation continues in parallel. Uthmeier says other states will follow.
The Florida Docket tracks the case that asks whether AI companies are manufacturers, whether manufacturers have duties, and whether a CEO can be held personally liable for the design choices of a product his company built and sold to children.

name: The Great Canadian Trade War
description:
Trade Wars & Economic Reality
When the rhetoric doesn't match the math
A deep dive into the numbers behind today's biggest trade disputes. We cut through political theater to analyze what the data actually shows—from fentanyl seizures that don't justify trillion-dollar trade wars to free trade agreements that quietly protect economies while politicians rage on social media.
If you've ever wondered whether the trade war headlines match the economic reality, this is where we do the math that matters.

name: The Great Energy Challenge: Power, Policy, and the Technologies Reshaping America
sections: The Great Energy Challenge: Power, Policy, and the Technologies Reshaping America
description: From AI's insatiable power appetite to the electric vehicle transition, from battery revolutions to government-sponsored sabotage of clean energy — this series tracks the defining industrial challenge of our era: whether the United States will build the energy future, or pay someone else's price for refusing to.

name: The Great Gayermandering Series
description: The Great Gayermandering Series is a three-part political satire exploring what happens when desperate politicians take gerrymandering to its most absurd extreme. Part 1 introduces Texas's fictional "gayermandering" scheme that draws district lines to exclude neighborhoods based on ridiculous cultural markers like coffee shop preferences and home décor choices. Part 2: Fifty Shades of Gerrymander chronicles how this madness spreads nationwide, with each state adding its own twist—from Missouri's "Anthropologie shopping pattern" districts to Ohio's AI-drawn maps based on Skyline Chili consumption. Part 3: The Reckoning examines the national fallout, legal chaos, and international embarrassment as America's redistricting arms race threatens to make democracy itself a joke. While satirical, the series is uncomfortably close to reality—the actual gerrymandering happening in 2025 is nearly as absurd as the fiction, which is exactly the point.

name: The Grievance Machine
description:
In November and December of 2020, Donald Trump told the country an American election could not be trusted — and named the exact mechanisms he blamed: the machines, the mail ballots, the voter rolls, the count itself. Every claim went to court. Almost none of them held up, including before judges he appointed.

In 2025 and 2026, holding the office he once said had been stolen from him, Trump built federal control over those same mechanisms — not to make them more trustworthy, but to make them answerable to him. This five-part series lays out both records side by side: what he claimed when he lost, and what he built once he couldn't lose again without a fight. No verdict is offered until the final essay. The evidence, assembled in full, is asked to make its own case first.

name: The Guardian: Khamenei's Iran - From Revolutionary Promise to Authoritarian Collapse
sections: The Guardian: Khamenei's Iran - From Revolutionary Promise to Authoritarian Collapse
description:
For 37 years, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has ruled Iran as Supreme Leader, claiming to guard the Islamic Revolution's values. In June 2025, he spent twelve days hiding in an underground bunker while Israeli and American forces bombed his nuclear facilities. By January 2026, Iranians across all 31 provinces are demanding his overthrow.
This 12-part investigative series examines Khamenei's rule not through Western perspectives, but by the revolution's own standards—the promises made in 1979 and the principles he claims to uphold. From systematic repression through five major protest movements, to economic devastation, military humiliation, and the current uprising, we document how the "Guardian" betrayed every revolutionary promise.
Using his own words, his own standards, the evidence is damning.
The bunker awaits.

name: The Hermit Kingdom Ascendant
description:
In 2025, Kim Jong-un stood on a Beijing balcony alongside Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping — not as a supplicant, but as a peer. The man the world had spent thirty years predicting would collapse had instead ascended.
How did that happen?
The short answer involves a pandemic, a war in Ukraine, and a nuclear weapons programme built in defiance of every sanction the international community could devise. The long answer begins four thousand years ago, on a peninsula that has always been the most dangerous piece of real estate in Northeast Asia — squeezed between China, Russia, and Japan, fought over by every empire that ever rose in the region, and schooled by that experience in a form of strategic stubbornness that the world has consistently underestimated.
The Hermit Kingdom Ascendant traces North Korea from its ancient origins to its emergence as a nuclear power — the history that explains the headlines, and the headlines that vindicate the history.

name: The Hinton Lectures: Three Nights in Toronto
sections: The Hinton Lectures: Three Nights in Toronto
description: Every November the AI Safety Foundation brings a leading thinker on artificial intelligence to Toronto for three public lectures named for Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel laureate who helped build modern A.I. and now warns where it is heading. In 2026 the lecturer was Paul Christiano, a founder of the field of A.I. alignment who pioneered at OpenAI the training technique that made chatbots safe enough to release. On November 9, 10 and 11 he made his case in three steps: why A.I. systems might try to take control, why they may soon be able to, and what we should do about it. His answer: slow down now, so that we can slow down later. The Hinton Lectures is a sub-series of The AI Trials and Tribulations. It records each night, in Christiano’s own words where possible, with Hinton’s responses, written in collaboration with Claude.

name: The House Built for Winter
description:
A series on the world we built, the climate that is leaving it, and what comes next.

The British build their houses to hold heat. Four centuries of damp northern winters taught them to prize warmth and hoard it — thick brick, small windows, the carpet running wall to wall. It was wisdom. This summer, as France logged its hottest day in recorded history and Britain issued its rarest heat warnings, that wisdom turned lethal: the houses built to trap heat trapped it, and the people inside cooked.

That is this series, in one image. We are a civilization living inside infrastructure — physical, legal, financial, political — calibrated to a climate that is quietly walking out the door. The houses. The insurance markets. The water treaties. The energy grids. All of it built, sensibly, for a world we no longer have.

This is a Canadian's look at what happens when the world changes and the bricks don't.

name: The Household Ledger
description:
Every household keeps a ledger, whether anyone calls it that or not — a chequebook, a banking app, the mental arithmetic done in a grocery aisle when a familiar item costs more than it did last month. It is the truest economic indicator most people will ever consult, because it cannot be revised away or spun in a press briefing.

This series exists because that ledger has been telling an uncomfortable story for a great many American households, at the exact moment the economy has become the single issue voters say matters most heading into November — and the exact moment the president insists there is nothing to worry about at all.

The Household Ledger follows the Federal Reserve, tariffs, groceries, housing, and credit costs back to where they actually land: a kitchen table. Weekly, through the midterms.

name: The Hypocrisy Chronicles: Inside the 2025 Shutdown
sections: The Hypocrisy Chronicles: Inside the 2025 Shutdown
description: This multipart-part series follows the money, the blame, the propaganda, and the escalating cruelty of the October 2025 government shutdown—using the administration's own words, actions, and deleted documents to expose how 42 million Americans became pawns in Trump's war against Democratic leadership.

name: The Hypocrisy of Donald Trump and His Administration
short: The Hypocrisy of Donald Trump and His Administration
sections: The Hypocrisy of Donald Trump and His Administration
aliases: The Hypocrisy of Donald Trump and His Administration
description: This multi-part investigation examines how the Trump administration systematically exploits tragedy, sanitizes extremism, and abandons intellectual consistency for political advantage. Written from the perspective of demanding evidence-based reasoning from political leaders, the series documents how Trump weaponizes memorial services, eulogies, and public sympathy to normalize positions that contradict his own documented record. Through policy analysis and examination of documented statements, it reveals the difference between genuine leadership and political opportunism, showing how the sanitization of extremism damages democratic discourse and public trust.

name: The Impossible Democracy
description:
There are five languages spoken in my Toronto townhouse on any given morning. Dzongkha, Gujarati, Punjabi, Hindi, and English — three countries, four men, one coffee maker, and a spice shelf that requires occasional diplomacy.
I have been sharing a kitchen with Indian men for the better part of two decades. The lesson has been consistent and unavoidable: India is not one thing. It is twenty-eight states, twenty-two official languages, and more internal diversity than all of Europe combined. It is the world's largest democracy, built on a constitution written by an Untouchable, surviving Partition, assassination, emergency rule, and the rise of Hindu nationalism — and somehow, noisily, imperfectly, still holding together.
This series asks a simple question: How?
The Impossible Democracy begins Friday. Written from the only vantage point I trust — not above, not inside, but alongside.

name: The Iran Crisis
description:
The Iran Crisis Series began in December 2025, documenting the protests that erupted across Iran after a currency crash on December 28 — and how Trump's Venezuela invasion changed the calculations of both protesters and the regime. Those eight essays traced the economic collapse, the massacre hidden behind an internet blackout, and the perverse incentive driving Iran toward nuclear weapons as the only deterrent against American intervention.
On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury. The series became something else.
What follows is a day-by-day record of the first major American war in the Middle East since Iraq — its casualties, its contradictions, its civilian cost, and the strategic consequences no one in Washington has yet named honestly.

name: The Kash Patel Files
description:
According to reporting by The Atlantic — sourced to more than two dozen current and former officials — the director of the FBI has consumed alcohol to the point that his security detail considered requesting breaching equipment to reach him. The New York Times has reported that he assigned a SWAT team to escort his girlfriend to hair appointments and that his staff physically prevented him from posting classified photographs of allied intelligence chiefs on social media. He has publicly acknowledged firing agents for cases they were assigned to work. He has done all of this during a war with Iran.
This series examines what may be the most comprehensively documented leadership failure in modern American law enforcement — drawn from open-source reporting and the testimony of dozens of FBI officials who broke the bureau's code of silence because staying silent had become more dangerous than speaking.
He should be worried. So should we.

name: The Long Return
description: For most of recorded history, China was the centre of the known world — the Middle Kingdom, Zhōngguó, a name that was never meant as metaphor. Then came the opium wars, the unequal treaties, the century the Chinese still call national humiliation, and a fall from centrality so complete it took a revolution, a famine, a cultural purge, and forty years of relentless reform to reverse. The Long Return traces that arc: from Zheng He's treasure fleets at the height of Ming power, through the wreckage of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, to Deng's pivot, Tiananmen's shadow, and Xi Jinping's consolidation. It ends where The Quiet War begins — with the 141 pages. This is the foundation the rest of the section rests on: not just what China is doing now, but why it believes it has earned the right to do it.

name: The Masculinity Con: Inside the Tate Brothers’ £21 Million Exploitation Machine
sections: The Masculinity Con: Inside the Tate Brothers’ £21 Million Exploitation Machine
description: In a bombshell Dec. 10, 2025, NYT investigation, reporters Megan Twohey and Isabella Kwai published the sealed Romanian indictment and exposed Trump administration officials overriding prosecutors to free Andrew and Tristan Tate.These six essays go deeper: the Tate case is proof-of-concept for the global export of Trump’s accountability-evasion system—alleged romance fraud, violence, £21 million in porn profits, rebranded as “defending masculinity,” backed by conservative media and direct political protection.Deliver a voting bloc, play the culture-war martyr, and justice becomes optional. The Tates got rich and taught thousands the playbook.How many are already copying it?

name: The Middle Kingdom
description:
China calls itself Zhōngguó — the Middle Kingdom — a name that has carried the weight of civilisational self-perception for millennia. It is not a boast. It is a cosmology. For most of recorded history, China was the centre of the known world. Then it wasn't. Then it decided to become so again.
This section examines that arc. The Quiet War tracks the strategic competition happening right now — the Five-Year Plan, the rare earths, the quantum networks, the robot armies. Formosa: The Beautiful Problem examines the unresolved territorial claim where that competition is most likely to turn hot. The Long Return traces how China became the country capable of all of it — from the Ming treasure fleets to the 141 pages.
I have visited China multiple times, always with fascination. The scale impresses. The grip is real. A friend in Shenzhen stopped replying to my essays. He didn't need to explain why. That silence is what this section is about.

name: The Ministry of Truth
description: In Orwell's 1984, the Ministry of Truth was where the Party rewrote history and manufactured propaganda while calling it fact. Today, we're watching something equally perverse: those who spent years crying "fake news" about actual journalism are now creating literal state propaganda and calling it truth. This section tracks the inversion—the moments when words lose all meaning, when "transparency" means censorship, when asking questions becomes a crime, and when propaganda outlets are celebrated as honest journalists while real reporters are cast out. Welcome to the Ministry of Truth, where the biggest lie is in the name itself.

name: The Musk Stack Substack
description: Elon Musk holds simultaneous control over aerospace, satellite telecommunications, social media, artificial intelligence, automotive manufacturing, humanoid robotics, and energy infrastructure. No individual in history has held leverage across this many domains simultaneously. This 12 part series traces how a South African teenager — shaped by Douglas Adams's galactic imagination and driven by an engineer's insistence on reasoning from first principles — used a Canadian passport to reach America and built the most concentrated portfolio of strategic power the modern world has seen. It also asks where first principles thinking ends and something else begins. Written from Canada, the country that gave Musk his first citizenship and his pathway to everything that followed.

name: The Name Game
description:
Donald Trump has spent a lifetime writing his name on things. Towers. Golf courses. Hotels. A university. A Bible. A perfume called Success. A peace institute he gutted before the paint on the letters dried. A performing arts centre dedicated to a murdered president he has spent his entire career trying to impress.
The name is always the same: gold where possible, large where mandatory, permanent where permitted, and imposed where neither permission nor permanence was ever his to grant.
This series is about what that compulsion reveals — psychologically, politically, historically, and occasionally comically. It is not a flattering portrait.
Then again, neither is a loading dock on Bay Street.
The Name Game is a ten-part series examining Donald Trump's lifelong obsession with seeing himself everywhere — and what happens when the world finally says no.

name: The Neverendum Story
description:
Canada's long argument with itself. Again? Must be Tuesday.

On October 5, 2026, Quebecers voted in an election the Parti Québécois was favoured to win on a promise of a third sovereignty referendum. Fourteen days later, Albertans vote on whether to begin the legal process toward one of their own. Somewhere between Gaspé and Grande Prairie, a man in a Tim Hortons looks up from his double-double and says, "Again? Must be Tuesday."

He has a point. Canada has been threatening to come apart since roughly the morning after it was assembled, and it remains, stubbornly, in one piece. This series asks why. It follows separatism from Nova Scotia's 1868 repeal campaign through the Quiet Revolution, two Quebec referendums and four decades of Western alienation, to the courtroom rules that now govern any exit and the American officials now taking meetings. What did the separatists want? What did they win without leaving? And is the national shrug wisdom, or luck?

name: The New Camelot
description: New York's 12th District — the smallest, richest, most educated congressional seat in America — is holding a primary that money can't buy and nobody can predict. A Kennedy grandson, a Republican defector, a former child magician, and a tech defector are competing for a seat that defines itself by being undefinable. A Canadian watches from across the border, remembering a thirteen-year-old boy shot in Dallas, and wondering what his legacy has become.

name: The Noem Files
description: On January 7, 2026, an ICE agent shot and killed Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old American mother, in Minneapolis. DHS Secretary Kristi Noem immediately called it "domestic terrorism," claiming Good tried to ram federal agents. Video evidence proved this was a lie. Seventeen days later, Border Patrol agents killed Alex Jeffrey Pretti, a 37-year-old VA nurse who cared for veterans. DHS claimed he "wanted to massacre law enforcement." Video shows he approached with his phone to record them. They shot him ten times in five seconds. Two American citizens. Both 37. Both Minneapolis residents. Both killed by DHS. Both lied about immediately. Seventeen days apart. This series documents how Tom Ridge's 2001 vision—"protect Americans from terrorism"—became Kristi Noem's weapon that kills Americans and calls them terrorists. The normalization stops here.

name: The Nonpolitical Man: Life and Times of Anthony Fauci
sections: The Nonpolitical Man: Life and Times of Anthony Fauci
description:
For four decades, Anthony Fauci built the rarest thing in American public life: the trust of six presidents, two political parties, and a public that mostly agreed on almost nothing else. Then a pandemic made him famous, and fame did what it always eventually does to the trusted — it turned him into a symbol two sides could fight over, long after anyone remembered the man underneath.

This series is an attempt to recover that man. Not the sun god of science his admirers made him, nor the megalomaniac his critics have decided he always was — but the Jesuit-schooled researcher who quietly rebuilt American drug policy under fire from the AIDS activists who once called him a murderer, who helped save 25 million lives through PEPFAR, and who now sits, at 85, invoking the Fifth Amendment before a Senate more interested in a clip than an answer.

name: The Northern Mirror: How American Chaos Reveals Canadian Contradictions
sections: The Northern Mirror: How American Chaos Reveals Canadian Contradictions
description:
A 10-part series examining the uncomfortable truths that living next to the world's most scrutinized democracy reveals about Canadian politics, policy, and national character. From democratic deficits to policy mythology, from media blind spots to international hypocrisy—this series uses America as an unwitting mirror to expose the Canadian problems we'd rather not see. Because the first step toward fixing our issues is admitting they exist, and right now our smugness is preventing us from even seeing them.
New installments published weekly

name: The Numbers Game
description:
I count my essays. I have done this since the beginning, the way some people count steps, or the days since they quit something. Most of the time the number is just a number.

Every so often it isn’t. The count lands on a year that already means something — a conquest, a charter, a departure, a discovery — and I find myself writing about a king or a sailor or a teenager on horseback instead of whatever I’d planned for that day. I don’t choose these. I’ve tried, once, to engineer one onto its anniversary, and talked myself out of it before I’d gone very far. The numbers find me. I just notice when they do.

Some entries here are satire. Some aren’t satire at all. A few are the most personal things I write. The series has no fixed length and no fixed tone — only a promise to tell you, honestly, when I planned ahead and when I didn’t.

name: The Oakland Transcript
description:
The Oakland Transcript is a real-time diary of the Musk v. Altman trial — the most consequential corporate governance case in the history of artificial intelligence. It publishes as the proceedings warrant, for the duration of a trial expected to run through late May 2026.
Each dispatch synthesizes courtroom reporting from the journalists covering the trial in Oakland, read through the analytical framework built across thirty-one installments of The Asimov Gap — this Substack's ongoing series on AI governance and democratic accountability. You do not need to have read The Asimov Gap to follow The Oakland Transcript, but the two series are designed to be read together. Cross-references will guide you.
The trial will not resolve the AI governance crisis. It will not close the gap between what this technology can do and what any democratic institution is empowered to prevent. But it will produce a record. The record will matter. That is why this exists.

name: The Opera Cycle
description:
Every Trump–Xi summit is staged like a grand opera. This section reviews the performances, one summit at a time.

Since a private tour of the Forbidden City in 2017, every meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping has been produced with the care of a grand opera: venues chosen for their symbolism, pageantry rehearsed for weeks, and readouts written for two different audiences. This section follows the performances one summit at a time.

I. The Beijing Opera: Trump's state visit to China, May 2026.
II. The Washington Opera: Xi's return visit, September 2026.
III. The Shenzhen Opera: the APEC summit in Shenzhen, November 2026.
IV. The Miami Opera: the G20 in Miami, December 2026.

Each opera is a short series, written from Toronto by a Canadian in the cheap seats with a habit of keeping score. The TACO scorecard (Threaten, Accommodate, Capitulate, Obfuscate) runs through all of them, and every act asks the same question: who wrote the libretto, and who simply enjoyed the show?

name: The Pendulum and the Ratchet
description:
Americans like to say their politics swings like a pendulum: whatever goes out comes back. Edgar Allan Poe knew better. In his 1842 story, the blade above the prisoner swings back and forth, and with every swing it comes a little lower.

This series follows 88 policies, laws and institutions the Trump administrations have undone since 2017, from Title IX and fuel economy to the civil service, public lands and the independence of federal regulators. Fewer than half were Democratic creations. The rest were bipartisan, Republican, or older than party lines.

Each essay asks two questions. Can it be put back? And what is lost in the meantime? Some reversals can be undone with the stroke of a pen. Others are locked in place by Congress, the Supreme Court, signed contracts or simple physics.

A link to an interactive Reversal Ledger, updated as the courts rule, will be added to the Introduction essay

name: The Pinocchio Presidency
description: Welcome to the medical ward where political lies manifest as physical symptoms, where fact-checking becomes triage, and where the only cure is laughter mixed with horror. In this section, we chronicle the epidemic of normalized dishonesty through the lens of magical realism—because when a president tells his staff that "truth doesn't matter, only repetition does," perhaps the only sane response is insane satire. Each installment tracks the nasal growth patterns, symptomatic outbreaks, and democratic side effects of a post-truth presidency. Part medical journal, part fairy tale, part wake-up call, The Pinocchio Papers asks: When lying becomes as routine as breathing, what happens to the body politic? Bring your sense of humor and your sense of outrage—both are required for proper diagnosis.

name: The Pupusa Maker's Son
description: In March 2025, the Trump administration stuffed a construction worker named Kilmar Abrego Garcia on a plane and shipped him to the most notorious prison in the Western Hemisphere.
