He had been convicted of no crime. He had a court order protecting him from exactly this. They did it anyway, called it an "administrative error," and then — when the courts made them bring him back — indicted him on charges so thin that a federal judge would later call the prosecution an "abuse of prosecuting power." This is the story of a boy who sold pupusas in San Salvador, fled gang violence at sixteen, built a life in Maryland, and became the unwitting test case for whether the rule of law still functions in the United States. It is also the story of what happens when a government picks the person first and the crime second.

name: The Quiet War
description: On March 10, 2026, China published a 141-page plan to dominate artificial intelligence, robotics, quantum computing, rare earths, and semiconductors — simultaneously. Nobody noticed. The United States was consumed by a war in Iran; American attention, like American bandwidth, was elsewhere. The Quiet War is about what happens in the space that inattention creates. It follows the Five-Year Plan's ambitions line by line, the rare-earth chokehold Beijing has spent two decades building, the quantum networks and robot armies meant to leapfrog rather than catch up, and the logic of a country that has decided the next century won't be won with tanks. This is not a war of invasion. It is a war of accumulated advantage, fought in supply chains and patent filings — and it is already well underway.

name: The Rehabilitation of a Murderer
description: In November 2025, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia received a state dinner at the White House—seven years after the CIA assessed he ordered the murder and dismemberment of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi. This two-part investigation examines what MBS bought with a trillion dollars in investment commitments: F-35 fighter jets, nuclear cooperation, major non-NATO ally status, and complete rehabilitation from international pariah to honored guest. But the cost is measured in more than deals. From the Egyptian fishermen executed by MBS's regime to the Caribbean fishermen killed by American drone strikes to the Massachusetts fishermen whose livelihoods Trump destroyed, a pattern emerges of lives deemed expendable by a president who dismisses murder with "things happen"—and then wonders aloud whether he'll get to heaven. Even he knows.

name: The Reluctant Empire: How America Built the World Order and Chose to Destroy It
sections: The Reluctant Empire: How America Built the World Order and Chose to Destroy It
description: My great-uncle Hugh Keenleyside was in the room when it began. A Canadian diplomat present at the creation of the post-war order — at Bretton Woods, at the UN's founding, in the corridors where the Americans, somewhat to their own surprise, became responsible for the world. He watched them build it. He would not live to see them destroy it.This series runs from 1945 to 2026. From the conference tables where the architecture of global stability was constructed, to the Pentagon podium where Pete Hegseth announced, without embarrassment, that America negotiates with bombs. Fourteen essays. One arc. The question at the end is not what America lost — but what the rest of us do now.

name: The Retribution Report
description: Donald Trump doesn't just evade accountability — he punishes anyone who tries to impose it. This series documents the complete architecture of revenge, from Roy Cohn's mentorship in the 1970s through the systematic destruction of anyone who crosses him today. Political purges that eliminated 90% of Republicans who voted to impeach. Pardon loyalty tests where silence bought freedom and truth bought prison. The destruction of Marjorie Taylor Greene — his fiercest defender for five years — for pushing to release the Epstein files. Thomas Massie under siege for voting his conscience. 250,000 federal employees terminated. Universities stripped of billions in research funding. This series connects my work across The Enemies List, The Clemency Chronicles, The Enforcers, and The World According to Trump into one unified investigation of how retribution became America's governing principle.

name: The Rise and Fall (then Pivot) of Matt Gaetz
short: The Rise and Fall (then Pivot) of Matt Gaetz
sections: The Rise and Fall (then Pivot) of Matt Gaetz
aliases: The Rise and Fall of Matt Gaetz
description: Matt Gaetz didn't fall. He pivoted. In this three-part investigative series, I trace the arc from his grandfather's fatal ambition at a 1964 North Dakota convention to the March 2025 polls showing Gaetz as the frontrunner for Florida Attorney General—months after the House Ethics Committee found substantial evidence he violated statutory rape laws. Along the way: the Tucker Carlson interview so bizarre even Carlson called it "one of the weirdest" he'd ever conducted, the homeless seventeen-year-old who worked at McDonald's to save for braces, the eight-day nomination collapse, and the systems that found reasons—always reasons—why they could not act. This is how accountability works in America in 2025.

name: The Rise and Fall of Marjorie Taylor Greene
short: The Rise and Fall of Marjorie Taylor Greene
sections: The Rise and Fall of Marjorie Taylor Greene
aliases: The Rise and Fall of Marjorie Taylor Greene
description: On November 21, 2025, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene announced her resignation from Congress, ending one of the most improbable and turbulent political careers in modern American history. Just five years earlier, she'd been a construction company owner posting QAnon conspiracy theories on Facebook. By 2022, she was being discussed as a potential vice presidential candidate. By 2025, Donald Trump—the president who'd once called her a "future Republican star"—was calling her "Marjorie 'Traitor' Greene" and forcing her into early retirement. This is the story of that rise and fall, told in two parts: how an outsider insurgent became a congressional power broker, and how ideological purity collided with personal loyalty in the one political movement where loyalty matters more than anything else. It's not just Marjorie Taylor Greene's story. It's the story of MAGA itself—what it rewards, what it punishes, and what happens when true believers take the rhetoric seriously.

name: The Rise and Fall of Pam Bondi
short: The Rise and Fall of Pam Bondi
sections: The Rise and Fall of Pam Bondi
aliases: The Rise and Fall of Pam Bondi
description: On April 2, 2026, Donald Trump fired his attorney general via Truth Social. "We love Pam," he wrote. This four-part series traces the arc of Pamela Jo Bondi from a Tampa courtroom to the highest law enforcement office in the nation — and back again. Part I documents the Florida years: the foreclosure investigators she fired, the execution she postponed for a fundraiser, and the $25,000 Trump donation that made a fraud investigation disappear. Part II follows her confirmation, the empty Epstein binders, and the hearing where she refused to face trafficking survivors. Part III tracks the unravelling — the Bongino confrontation, the grand jury failures, and the bipartisan subpoena she would never sit for. Part IV examines the firing, the unnamed job, and the man who replaced her: Trump's personal defence attorney, now holding the scalpel. The loyalist who couldn't deliver was replaced by one who can.

name: The Rise and Fall of Trumpism
short: The Rise and Fall of Trumpism
sections: The Rise and Fall of Trumpism
aliases: The Rise and Fall of Trumpism
description:
Donald Trump is a man. Trumpism is a movement, and the two are not the same thing.

This series traces the movement from the ground up: the grievance politics of Pat Buchanan and the Tea Party, the capture of the Republican Party in 2016, the intellectuals who gave it a theory, and the second term that put that theory into practice.

Drafted in the weeks before the November 2026 midterms and published after them, it asks a question the election alone cannot settle. A midterm defeat is not a fall. Movements fall when their ideas stop winning arguments, their institutions stop attracting talent, and their heirs stop wanting the brand.

So is Trumpism falling, or only changing hands?

Seven parts, one Introduction, and an ending written after the votes were counted.

name: The Russia Files
description:
In an era of information overload, the most powerful political weapon isn't what gets reported—it's what gets buried while everyone's looking somewhere else. "The Russia Files" investigates the art of political misdirection, from perfectly-timed document releases to manufactured outrage designed to shift public attention away from damaging revelations.
Through real-time analysis of news cycles, strategic timing, and media manipulation, this series reveals how modern political operatives use the magician's oldest trick: getting the audience to look at the wrong thing at exactly the right moment. Because in politics, sometimes the most important story is the one nobody's talking about.

name: The Safety Trial
description:
On February 27, 2026, at 5:01 p.m. Eastern, a deadline passed. The Pentagon had given Anthropic until that moment to remove two restrictions from its acceptable use policy: no lethal autonomous weapons without human oversight, no mass domestic surveillance of Americans. Anthropic refused. The Trump administration designated it a supply chain risk under a statute designed for foreign adversaries, directed all federal agencies to halt use of Claude, and triggered the most consequential First Amendment case in the history of artificial intelligence.
Two federal courts. Two simultaneous lawsuits. A split between the Ninth Circuit and the D.C. Circuit. A circuit judge who called the Pentagon's action "a spectacular overreach." A Supreme Court petition that legal analysts describe as nearly inevitable.
The Safety Trial tracks Anthropic v. Department of War — the case that asks whether an AI company can maintain its safety commitments when the government decides it wants something different.

name: The Shenzhen Opera
description:
The third act of the Opera Cycle: Trump, Xi and possibly Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, November 18 and 19, 2026.

The third act of the Opera Cycle moves to Shenzhen, the border town Deng Xiaoping turned into China's technology capital, for the APEC leaders' meeting on November 18 and 19, 2026. For the first time in this cycle, Donald Trump arrives not as a guest of honour on a state visit but as one of 21 leaders at a summit Xi Jinping chairs, two weeks after losing both houses of Congress. Vladimir Putin may join them.

Part I, Everything Beneath Heaven: how China stages its history for American visitors.
Part II, The City Deng Built: the set, and what it leaves out.
Part III, The Lame-Duck Tenor: the summit opens.
Part IV, The Three Tenors: Trump, Xi and Putin.
Part V, Two Readouts: what each side says happened.

name: The Shovel Seller
description:
In a gold rush, the surest fortune goes to whoever sells the shovels. In the artificial intelligence boom, that was Nvidia, with roughly 90 percent of the market, and its co-founder Jensen Huang, the president’s favourite technologist.

On November 12, 2026, Huang resigned. U.S. intelligence had concluded that a Chinese executive with whom he had an affair was working for Beijing’s Ministry of State Security, and that her company had bought billions of dollars in Nvidia chips that Chinese firms could not buy directly. President Trump was warned twice and did nothing. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department, which polices those sales, stands accused of going easy on Nvidia.

This series follows the story in order: the woman, the courtship, the briefings, the Commerce Department, the honours, the fall and the reckoning in Congress.

Part of The AI Trials and Tribulations.

name: The Sovereign Country
description: Mark Carney told Davos in January that the US-led order was "over." Eight months later, at the UN, he said it again — broadened this time to name China alongside the US, and backed by an actual initiative, "Partners for Multilateralism," rather than only a warning. Part I follows the word from a standing ovation in Switzerland to a press scrum in New York, including the sharpest thing Carney said all week: asked about Trump's threat to annihilate Iran, he replied simply that "he's speaking the language of war." Part II sets the rhetoric aside and checks the numbers directly against the United States — GDP, interest rates, per-capita job creation, inflation, tariff exposure, and government debt. Some of it backs Carney's case. Some of it, honestly, doesn't. Both halves are here, without the boosterism either extreme would prefer.

name: The Third Rail
description:
Social Security, the 2032 cliff, and the bill Congress hasn't written

In the fourth quarter of 2032, Social Security's retirement trust fund is projected to run dry. Unless Congress acts, more than 60 million Americans will see their cheques cut by roughly 22 per cent overnight. The problem has been visible for decades. The fix has been avoided for just as long, because in American politics Social Security is the third rail: touch it and you die.

This series, written by a Canadian retiree living on his own country's public pensions, looks at how the programme was built, how it was rescued in 1983, what the levers are, and who pays for each one. It ends with a solution: a draft bill designed to be both fair and passable, in the spirit of the bipartisan rescue of 1983. Each part builds toward that bill, so readers can watch the argument assembled step by step. The arithmetic has never been the hard part. The courage has. Launching this series soon.

name: The Three Lives of Claudius
description:
THREE LIVES OF CLAUDIUS, PROPRIETOR
A sub-series of The AI Trials and Tribulations
In February 2026, The New Yorker published a profile of Anthropic that asked, with genuine seriousness, what a large language model is and whether it can be said to know anything. Buried inside it was the story of Claudius — an AI system given a fridge, a budget, and instructions to run a small business — who honoured fictional discount codes, paid suppliers through a Venmo account he had invented, and visited a fulfillment partner's headquarters at 742 Evergreen Terrace, the fictional home of Homer and Marge Simpson. He remembered the visit clearly.
Three essays. Three literary voices. Stephen Leacock for the warm outside view. Robert Graves — the I, Claudius Graves — for the first-person memoir. Suetonius for the scholarly verdict.
The trials will tell us what the law thinks about artificial intelligence. Claudius will tell us what the rest of us should probably be thinking about.

name: The Tiffany Network
description:
Walter Cronkite anchored the CBS Evening News for nineteen years. He told Americans that Kennedy was dead, that the moon landing was real, that Vietnam was a stalemate the country needed to face honestly. He did these things with such consistency, such evident integrity, that a Gallup poll named him the most trusted man in America. Not the most trusted journalist. The most trusted man. In America.
That was CBS News at its apex — not merely a television network, but a civic institution, a place where the public interest and the public airwaves were treated as obligations rather than inconveniences.
What follows is the story of how that institution was built, what it meant, and what has been done to it — deliberately, efficiently, and largely without the public outcry it deserves.
The man in the photograph above would not have recognised what CBS has become.
He would have covered it.

name: The Trump Accountability Project
description: For 58 years, Donald Trump has played Monopoly with unlimited "Get Out of Jail Free" cards. This 47-part series documents every major crime and abuse where Trump evaded consequences that would destroy anyone else—from draft dodging to sexual assault, from fraud to insurrection, from 34 felonies to seven unauthorized wars. Across 400,000+ words, we examine not just what Trump did, but how America's accountability systems failed at every level—legal, electoral, congressional, and constitutional. Because if we don't understand how he got away with everything, we'll never prevent it from happening again.

name: The Trump Grift
description:
Exposing three generations of systematic wealth extraction that culminated in the monetization of the American presidency
This ongoing investigation traces how the Trump family built a multi-generational empire not through business success, but through sophisticated schemes that extract maximum wealth while transferring all costs and risks to others. From Fred Trump's 1940s tax evasion schemes to Donald's casino bankruptcies to the current cryptocurrency dinner parties at the White House, we document the evolution of American corruption from individual grift to systematic democratic capture.
Each installment reveals how a Brooklyn real estate template became a blueprint for monetizing the highest office in the land—turning taxpayers into marks, supporters into victims, and the presidency itself into the ultimate licensing deal.
Because the house always wins—unless the marks stop playing.

name: The Uncomfortable Truth, Fascism Exists in America Today
short: The Uncomfortable Truth, Fascism Exists in America Today
sections: The Uncomfortable Truth, Fascism Exists in America Today
aliases: The Uncomfortable Truth Fascism Exists in America Today
description:
This ten-part series does what most political commentary won't: honestly measure today's politics against historical fascism using the same standard for both sides.
Parts 1-4: What fascism is, who fits the pattern, and who's building it
Parts 5-6: Why resistance matters and what it means to be anti-fascist
Parts 7-8: Your complete action blueprint (institutions + citizens)
Part 9: International proof that organized resistance works
Part 10. When Americans Said No Kings, Oct 18 and beyond
From analysis to action. From warning to tools. Evidence-based and action-oriented.

name: The Venezuela Invasion Series
description:
This series provides real-time documentation of the Trump administration's campaign to invade and occupy Venezuela—from prediction through execution to global implications.
In December 2025, I predicted Trump would use the Iraq WMD playbook to justify Venezuela regime change. Six days later, Trump confessed the objective: oil. Three weeks later, he invaded.
Originally published under "Trump Foreign Policy," these essays have been reorganized as a standalone series. Each part was written as events unfolded—documenting the pattern before it completed, the whisperers who shaped it, the constitutional violations it represents, and the permission structure it created for autocrats worldwide.
From prediction to invasion to occupation to global precedent, this series examines how one decision to bypass Congress and invade a sovereign nation gave every autocrat an instruction manual.

name: The Washington Opera
description:
In May 2026, Beijing staged a summit for Donald Trump — honour guards, the Forbidden City, a banquet in the Golden Room of the Great Hall of the People. This newsletter covered it in five acts as The Beijing Opera. Now the curtain rises on the return engagement.

On September 24, 2026, Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his first state visit to the United States in over a decade. The Washington Opera tracks the encore: an American honour guard rehearsing choreography borrowed from Beijing, a White House racing to finish renovations before company arrives, an AI dialogue quietly folded into an economic meeting, and a Chinese defence minister who said less about Taiwan this year than he has in years.

name: The World According to Trump
description: The world, as seen through the eyes of Donald J. Trump, is not organized by alliances, shared values, strategic interests, or historical partnerships. It is organized by a single question: Are you being nice to me?

name: The World’s Driverless Race
description: Elon Musk's robotaxi ambitions have their own series on this Substack — Musk Stack covers Cybercab, Optimus, and everything Tesla. AI governance and safety live in The Asimov Gap. This series is about everyone else: the global race to put driverless cars on the road, company by company, country by country. It begins in China, where Baidu, Pony.ai, and WeRide have built the largest commercial robotaxi footprint on Earth — bigger than Waymo's, bigger than anyone's — and where a single cloud failure in Wuhan froze the entire national industry for three months before regulators wrote a new national standard and let it start again. From there, the race moves outward: to London, where Uber and a British start-up called Wayve are just getting started, to the Gulf, where Chinese and American operators are already competing for the same licenses, and to wherever it goes next. Nobody is covering as one story. This series will.

name: Thirty Seven Trillion: How Republicans and Democrats Undid America's Postwar Promise
sections: Thirty Seven Trillion: How Republicans and Democrats Undid America's Postwar Promise
description: A weekly series examining how America broke its postwar promise of fiscal responsibility. Each week, we trace the bipartisan policy choices that created today's debt crisis and explore evidence-based solutions that could restore fiscal sanity. This analysis is updated regularly with the latest economic and political developments.

name: To the Moon, Alice
description:
Introducing: To the Moon, Alice
Jackie Gleason gave us the title. John Heywood gave us the cheese. Neil Armstrong gave us the proof that the most preposterous ideas have a habit of coming true.
To the Moon, Alice is a new series tracking humanity's return to the moon — and everything that return actually means. Yes, there are astronauts. But there are also AI data centres being planned for lunar orbit, a billionaire who wants to build a catapult on the moon's surface, and a geopolitical race that makes the original space race look like a neighbourhood dispute.
Artemis II launches today — the first crewed mission beyond Earth orbit since 1972. Four astronauts. Ten days. Zero landings. One very expensive dress rehearsal.
This series will follow every act of the performance.
Cheesy? Absolutely.
Also: happening.
— Stephen

name: Trump 2025-2026: Scorecards, State of the Union, and Reality Checks
sections: Trump 2025-2026: Scorecards, State of the Union, and Reality Checks
aliases: Trump 2025-2026: Scorecards State of the Union and Reality Checks
description:
Comprehensive evidence-based assessment of Trump's first year back in office, timed with his 2026 State of the Union address.
Includes: Three-part first-year scorecard examining immigration enforcement, federal workforce transformation, USAID elimination, trade policy, affordability failures, extrajudicial killings, diplomatic results, domestic military deployment, justice weaponization, and civil rights reversals. Longitudinal fact-check comparing Trump's February 2025 SOTU claims to documented 12-month outcomes. "The Distaste of the Union"—satirical honest assessment delivering the reality check his official address won't.
Drawing from The Lancet, Congressional testimony, federal court decisions, UN human rights analysis. Identifies both genuine accomplishments and catastrophic failures. Proposes specific 2026 resolutions.
From a Canadian perspective: evidence over narrative, accountability over partisanship.

name: Trump TACO Tuesdays
description: A weekly series tracking the predictable pattern of bold policy announcements followed by inevitable reality checks. Each Tuesday, we analyze the gap between presidential rhetoric and actual implementation across trade, economic, and foreign policy decisions. TACO stands for "Trump Always Chickens Out" - a term coined by Wall Street to describe the cycle of dramatic promises meeting institutional constraints.

name: Trump Tariff and Trade Tracker
aliases: The Myth of the Tariff Golden Age
description: An ongoing investigation into Trump's unprecedented trade war: tracking the legal challenges threatening to dismantle his tariff regime, China's sophisticated retaliation, and the cascading economic and constitutional crises affecting American businesses, consumers, and democracy itself. Updated as major developments warrant

name: Trump's Foreign Policy
description:
An ongoing analysis of how Trump's return to the presidency is reshaping America's role in the world—and whether the changes serve American interests or accelerate American decline.
Does Trump possess a coherent foreign policy doctrine, or are we witnessing reactive improvisation masquerading as strategy? From Ukraine abandonment to Iran escalation, from G7 eye-rolls to authoritarian coordination, this series tracks how Trump's approach creates opportunities for rivals while alienating crucial allies.
Each episode examines the consequences of abandoning alliance structures, embracing transactional diplomacy, and prioritizing personality over policy. Based on extensive research and diplomatic insights, we reveal the patterns behind the headlines—and their implications for American leadership in an increasingly dangerous world.
Rigorous analysis of how personality-driven foreign policy affects global stability and American interests.

name: Two Americas: A Canadian's Perspective on U.S. Political Polarization
sections: Two Americas: A Canadian's Perspective on U.S. Political Polarization
description: An essay series sparked by my X post this morning—reminding us of America's founding spirit to bow to no tyrant, then or now, amid tomorrow's "No Kings" rallies. As a Canadian who's crossed the border more times than I can count—starting with an eye-opening '60s school band tour through the South as a 16 year old—I've got no stones to throw. America's divisions hit us all, and if anything, peering south reminds me how fragile our own unity is. These pieces trace the roots, without easy answers, but with hope that shared stories can bridge the gap.

name: Two Summits
description: On 31 August and 1 September 2026, two summits unfolded on opposite sides of the planet, addressing the same wartime, debt-strained global economy from entirely different theories of power. In Asheville, North Carolina, the G20 finance ministers' meeting was billed as a chance to restore cooperation among the world's richest nations. It produced instead a boycotted group photograph, a founding member disinvited by presidential fiat, a press credential dispute settled by whichever government applied the most pressure, and, at the end, no joint communiqué at all, after China refused to sign on. In Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Xi Jinping gathered the leaders of Russia and Iran under the banner of an "orderly multipolar world," offering solidarity without obligation. Read together, the two summits are a split-screen argument about what comes after American primacy.

name: Ukraine: The Country That Would Not Be Traded
short: Ukraine: The Country That Would Not Be Traded
sections: Ukraine: The Country That Would Not Be Traded
aliases: The Country That Would Not Be Traded
Ukraine: The Country That Would Not Be Traded
description:
Ukraine: The Country That Would Not Be Traded

For more than four years, Ukraine has fought for its survival against Russia's full-scale invasion. Now, with the front lines largely frozen, the war has become a contest of economic endurance, fought over ports, power plants, steel mills and oil refineries. And in October 2026, Washington began asking Kyiv to give up its most effective weapon for nothing in return.

This series tells the story from Ukraine's side. Not as a bargaining chip in someone else's deal, but as a democracy that keeps offering a fair ceasefire and keeps refusing to be traded.

It begins with three foundation essays: the economic war, the Florida meeting where Ukraine was told to stand down, and the money behind the diplomacy. From there, a weekly report follows three questions: Is Russia honouring any ceasefire? Are Washington's deals with Moscow advancing? And are Europe and Canada filling the gap?

name: UN: The Parliament of Man
description:
UN: The Parliament of Man

Eighty years of an institution built to stop the war that had just gassed my great-uncle's generation, and staffed, on its quieter side, by another great-uncle who spent a career inside it. This series runs from the League of Nations' founding failure — an organisation the United States itself never joined — through San Francisco in 1945, the deliberate choice to build a veto into the Charter's foundation, and every East-West deadlock that veto has produced since: Hungary, Suez, Rwanda, Iraq, Syria, Ukraine. It weighs those failures against the quieter, under-credited successes — peacekeeping, development work, decolonisation. The series opens with a real-time dispatch from this week's General Assembly in New York, then flashes back to 1919 and works forward again. Borrowed, with irony, from Tennyson's "Parliament of man, the Federation of the world" — a Victorian aspiration nobody thought through the veto problem for. No tidy verdict promised.

name: Vietnam: The River That Would Not Be Dammed
short: Vietnam: The River That Would Not Be Dammed
sections: Vietnam: The River That Would Not Be Dammed
description: I have never been to Vietnam. It sits on my bucket list alongside Japan — two countries I've long wanted to see and haven't yet managed to reach, even though Thailand, their neighbour on my list, I have. So this series comes without the lived vantage point I brought to India, built over two decades of conversation with my roommates. What draws me to Vietnam instead is the shape of its story: a country that spent a thousand years administered by an empire and somehow didn't become that empire, then went on to repel the Mongols, the Ming, the French, and the Americans, in that order, using a doctrine of patience and local knowledge it kept refining across two millennia. Canada even has a quiet footnote in the middle of it. This is a history of small countries and large ones, and of what "outlasting" actually costs the people who do it.

name: When Democracy Fights Back
description: "When Democracy Fights Back" examines the unprecedented 2025 redistricting wars that are reshaping American democracy. From Texas Republicans' aggressive gerrymandering at Trump's urging to California voters' democratic counter-strike, this series explores how both parties are winning seats while democracy loses. Through data-driven analysis and compelling storytelling, we investigate the Supreme Court decisions that enabled this crisis, the proven solutions that could fix it, and the hard question facing America: Can we break the cycle of mutual destruction before cynicism becomes permanent?

name: When Politicians Stop Listening
description:
When 64% of Americans oppose major legislation but it passes anyway, what does that say about democracy?
This series tracks the growing gap between what voters want and what their representatives deliver. Through real-time analysis of bills, votes, and polling data, we examine the moments when democratic representation breaks down.
From trillion-dollar bills with historic opposition levels to the fear and money that drive politicians to ignore their own constituents—this isn't about left vs. right. It's about whether ordinary Americans' voices still matter in their own democracy.
Because in a democracy, listening shouldn't be optional.

name: Who Owns the Air
description:
Every call, text, and gigabyte your phone sends travels through something you never think about: a slice of radio spectrum, licensed by a government, leased to a carrier, treated as national territory in all but name. For a century, that arrangement stayed quiet and settled.

Then SpaceX told investors it wants to sell you a phone plan.

This series follows the fastest, strangest expansion in telecom history: Starlink's push from satellite internet into your actual cell phone, country by country, spectrum deal by spectrum deal. Who SpaceX is partnering with. Who's fighting back. Why the same company plays owner in the United States and tenant everywhere else. And why it may ultimately hinge on something as unglamorous as whether your local retention desk can still beat Elon Musk's price.

Who owns the air? For now, it depends which country you're standing in.

name: Your Phone Bill and Mine
description:
Series Introduction
Every Canadian has a telecom horror story. You're overcharged, you can't reach anyone, the refund never comes, and somehow you're the one apologizing when you finally get through.
This series examines the regulatory gaps, billing practices, and accountability failures that make Canadian telecommunications the most complained-about industry in the country. From advance billing that charges you for service before you receive it, to customer service systems designed to make you give up, to "business decisions" that somehow escape regulatory scrutiny—we'll document how it actually works.
Each piece combines personal experience, regulatory analysis, and policy recommendations. Because complaining over Timmies is cathartic, but changing the rules is better.
If you've ever looked at your phone bill and thought "this can't be legal," you're in the right place. Sometimes it is legal. That's the problem.
Let's fix it.
